body.en: These topics are specific to Applications and Interpretation HL.

A Markov chain models a system that moves between a fixed set of states, where the probability of the next state depends only on the current one (not the history). If \(\mathbf{p}_n\) is the state-probability (column) vector at step \(n\) and \(T\) is the transition matrix (column \(j\) holds the probabilities of moving from state \(j\)), then:

\[\mathbf{p}_{n+1}=T\mathbf{p}_n\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathbf{p}_n=T^n\mathbf{p}_0.\]

A steady state \(\mathbf{s}\) satisfies \(T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}\) — it is an eigenvector of \(T\) with eigenvalue 1, normalised so its entries sum to 1. For a well-behaved (regular) chain, \(\mathbf{p}_n\to\mathbf{s}\) as \(n\to\infty\), regardless of the starting distribution \(\mathbf{p}_0\).

note.en: The transition matrix is T = [[P(A→A), 1−P(B→B)], [1−P(A→A), P(B→B)]]. body.en:
A graph consists of vertices and edges. Weighted graph: edges have assigned weights (distances, costs). Key algorithms:

Kruskal's algorithm — minimum spanning tree (MST): add edges in increasing weight, skip cycles. Prim's algorithm — MST from a vertex; add cheapest edge to tree at each step.

Dijkstra's algorithm — shortest path from a source vertex.

Euler circuit: traverses every edge exactly once; requires all vertices to have even degree.

Hamiltonian path: visits every vertex exactly once.

value.en: Each column is a probability distribution from a state
Euler path: all edges once; Hamiltonian: all vertices once

Given \(\dot{x}=3x-y,\;\dot{y}=2x\). Find equilibrium and classify stability.

Solution: Equilibrium: \(3x-y=0,\;2x=0\implies (0,0)\).

Jacobian eigenvalues: \(\lambda^2-3\lambda+2=0\implies\lambda=1,2\). Both positive → unstable node.

question.en: Practice: A network has weighted adjacency matrix \(W\). Explain how the minimum spanning tree algorithm (Kruskal's) differs from Dijkstra's algorithm.

solution.en: Kruskal's builds the MST by always adding the globally cheapest edge that does not form a cycle. Dijkstra's finds shortest paths from a single source, greedily updating distance estimates.
